citeAs: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang (2025). Training Software Engineering Agents and Verifiers with SWE-Gym. Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, Vancouver, Canada. PMLR 267.
creator: Jiayi Pan, Xingyao Wang, Graham Neubig, Navdeep Jaitly, Heng Ji, Alane Suhr, Yizhe Zhang (UC Berkeley, UIUC, CMU, Apple)
description: SWE-Gym is the first environment for training software engineering (SWE) agents, containing 2,438 real-world task instances sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories. Each instance comprises a Python codebase with an executable runtime environment, unit tests, and a task specified in natural language. It is designed to support training of language model-based SWE agents and verifiers through rejection sampling fine-tuning and inference-time scaling.
name: SWE-Gym
rai:annotatorDemographics: Annotations were done by a subset of the authors (researchers from UC Berkeley, UIUC, CMU, and Apple). No further demographic details are provided.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Validation was performed using SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script to ensure that the gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code. Instances that failed this validation were filtered out. The process required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours, resulting in 2,438 validated instances from 11 repositories.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations were performed by a subset of the authors. Dependencies for each task instance were manually configured using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script was used to ensure that the gold patch (the human-submitted code diff) passes more unit tests than the original code. The SWE-Gym Lite subset was delineated following the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline, excluding tasks that require editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, those with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation.
rai:dataBiases: The task distribution across repositories exhibits a long-tail pattern: tasks associated with pandas comprise nearly one-third of the total, whereas tasks related to bokeh represent a mere one percent. Tasks in SWE-Gym are on average harder than those in SWE-Bench, partly due to inclusion of sophisticated repositories like pandas and MONAI. Repeated sampling shows that task success probability follows a long-tail distribution, where more samples increase solved instances, introducing a bias toward easier tasks. The authors introduce per-instance capping to mitigate this bias. Ignoring executable environments could introduce distribution bias, which the authors address through manual configuration of dependencies.
rai:dataCollection: Task instances were sourced from pull requests in 11 popular Python repositories. The SEART GitHub search tool was used to filter repositories created before July 1, 2022 with more than 500 stars, at least 300 lines of code, more than 500 pull requests, and 100 contributors, yielding 358 repositories. SWE-Bench's instance extraction script was used to convert repositories into task instances, each corresponding to a GitHub issue including the natural language description, a snapshot of the repository, and a set of unit tests. Executable environments were manually configured using relevant configuration files (e.g., requirements.txt), CI scripts, or documentation from the repository snapshot at the time of issue creation. SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script was used to ensure that the gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code. The process required approximately 200 human annotation hours and 10,000 CPU core hours.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of GitHub pull requests and issues from 358 Python repositories. Over the 358 repositories, 64,689 task instances were extracted (referred to as SWE-Gym Raw), each containing code, issue descriptions, and the solution (git patch), but without executable environments or guaranteed effective unit tests.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Repositories created before July 1, 2022 were selected. The exact end date of data collection is not specified beyond this cutoff.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: SWE-Gym is limited by its environment diversity, including the number of repositories (11 with executable environments), types of tasks, and programming languages (Python only). The dataset currently contains 2,438 instances, which may limit training data scale. Performance is currently limited by the compute budget for sampling trajectories rather than the number of tasks. The self-improvement approach is not yet effective with rejection sampling fine-tuning alone. The dataset covers only Python repositories, limiting generalizability to other programming languages.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A subset of 230 tasks (SWE-Gym Lite) was identified following the SWE-Bench Lite filtering pipeline, excluding tasks requiring editing more than one file, tasks with poorly described problem statements, those with excessively complex ground-truth code diffs, and tests focused on error message validation. Per-instance capping was introduced to limit the maximum number of selected samples per task to mitigate bias toward easier tasks in trajectory datasets used for training.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Repositories were filtered using SEART GitHub search based on creation date (before July 1, 2022), star count (>500), lines of code (>300), pull requests (>500), and contributors (>100). SWE-Bench's instance extraction script was used to convert repositories into task instances. Instances were versioned using a generalized SWE-Bench versioning script. Executable environments were set up with pre-installed dependencies. SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script was used to verify that the gold patch passes more unit tests than the original code. Failed instances were filtered out, resulting in 2,438 validated instances from 11 repositories. Pre-built Docker images were created for each instance (totaling 6 TB).
rai:dataSocialImpact: Improving automated software engineering capabilities could increase developer productivity and accessibility across industries. Current models are primarily research artifacts and not yet production-ready, but can support critical open-source infrastructure and potentially make software development more accessible. As agents become more capable, they may impact software engineering jobs and require careful consideration around code ownership, licensing, and attribution. Similar techniques could potentially be misused to automate the creation of malicious code. The authors encourage future work to explore frameworks for responsible deployment, including considerations around security, safety, and economic impacts.
rai:dataUseCases: Training language model-based software engineering agents via rejection sampling fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. Training verifier (outcome-supervised reward) models for inference-time scaling. Enabling self-improvement of SWE agents through iterative rejection sampling fine-tuning. Benchmarking and rapid prototyping of SWE agents (via SWE-Gym Lite subset). Supporting research in automatic environment synthesis, self-improvement with reinforcement learning, and human-agent interaction for software engineering.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEART GitHub search tool was used to filter repositories. SWE-Bench's instance extraction script was used to convert repositories into task instances. SWE-Bench's versioning script (generalized) was used to associate instances with version numbers. SWE-Bench's execution-based validation script was used to verify gold patches. The Qwen-2.5-Coder-Instruct-7B tokenizer was used to estimate the number of tokens in trajectories.

null_reasons.rai:annotationsPerItem: The paper does not specify a number of independent annotations per item; environment setup was done once per instance by authors.
null_reasons.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: No external annotation platform was used; annotations were done by a subset of the authors directly.
null_reasons.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper does not explicitly discuss missing data handling beyond filtering out failed instances during validation.
null_reasons.rai:dataImputationProtocol: No imputation protocol is described; failed instances are filtered out rather than imputed.
null_reasons.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset consists of GitHub issues and code repositories; no personal or sensitive information is discussed.
null_reasons.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: No versioning, update cadence, or maintenance plan is described in the paper.
